newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's CVRD auction faces risk of further delay.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's CVRD auction faces risk of further delay.

text.p: The privatization of Brazilian mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) has been rescheduled for May 5, but a judge who is considering a key appeal to allow the sale has said he may only decide by May 6.

The auction, which has been rescheduled three times already, hinges on the verdict of high court judge Democrito Ramos Reinaldo who is to decide on a government appeal against lawsuits blocking the sale.
"It (the verdict) will probably have to wait until Tuesday," Reinaldo of the Superior Court of Justice, Brazil's highest court for nonconstitutional matters, told reporters Friday.
Latin America's largest privatization so far had originally been scheduled for April 29. But the auction was delayed first to April 30, then May 2 and now May 5 due to a slew of court injunctions.

The government is appealing to have all lawsuits against the CVRD sale handled by a single tribunal because of a "conflict of interpretation" in lower courts. It has also appealed to the Superior Court of Justice to overturn the existing injunctions granted by different courts.
If the sell-off cannot take place on Monday, the auction will be rescheduled again for each subsequent day, the Planning Ministry said.
More than 120 lawsuits have been filed against the company's privatization.
Seen as a key test to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's commitment to state reform, the sale of CVRD has raised considerable opposition from nationalists and leftists.

Opponents, from former presidents Itamar Franco and Jose Sarney to Brazil's Roman Catholic bishops, have accused the government of selling the country's mineral wealth to foreigners and private investors for a pittance.
The Carajas mine, CVRD's main asset, is the biggest iron ore deposit in the world with reserves of 18 billion metric tons.
With the sale of a 45 percent voting stake in CVRD, the government expects to raise at least $2.8 billion. If completed, the firm's privatization could net the government about $5 billion.

Two groups are ready to bid for the control of the mining conglomerate: one led by local steel firm CSN, and another headed by Brazil's largest private industrial conglomerate Grupo Votorantim and South Africa's Anglo-American Corp.
